pll1d9c4-d1e3477.summary: Raises the question: since the generation has no beginning or end, should one say the Son is always being begotten, always has been begotten, or will always be begotten?

pll1d9c4-d1e3480.summary: Cites Gregory's Moralia: the Lord was born of the Father before time, or rather, since he neither began nor ceased being born, more truly 'always born.' One cannot say 'always being born' lest he seem imperfect. 'Born' signifies perfection and 'always' eternity, though even 'perfect' falls short, since what was not made cannot properly be called perfect; we stammer about divine things.
claims: The Son is more truly said to be 'always born.'
'Always being born' would suggest imperfection.
Even calling the Son 'perfect' falls short of the truth.
Human speech about God is a kind of stammering.

pll1d9c4-d1e3520.summary: Cites Augustine on Ps 2:7: 'today' could refer to Christ's human birth, but since it signifies presence, and in eternity there is no past or future, it is better read of the eternal generation of Wisdom. 'I have begotten' excludes novelty; 'today' excludes pastness.
claims: 'Today' in Ps 2:7 signifies the eternal present.
The Son's generation is always, neither past nor future.

pll1d9c4-d1e3563.summary: Adds Chrysostom: the Prophet's words show only that the Son is always begotten from the Father's very essence.
claims: The Son is always begotten from the Father's essence.

pll1d9c4-d1e3578.summary: Cites Origen on Jeremiah: the Savior, as the brightness of eternal light, is not born once and finished but is always being born, as brightness arises whenever light does, hence 'he begets me' in the present. This seems to contradict Gregory's denial.
claims: Origen holds that the Son is always being born.
This seems to contradict Gregory's denial of 'semper nascitur.'

pll1d9c4-d1e3636.summary: Cites Augustine's 83 Questions: 'born' is better than 'always being born,' since what is always being born is never yet born. The Son is Son because born, and always Son because eternal, so always born.
claims: One who is always being born would never be born.
The Son is always born.

pll1d9c4-d1e3656.summary: Proposes to interpret Gregory charitably so that the great authorities do not seem to contradict each other on so great a matter.

pll1d9c4-d1e3672.summary: Reconciles them: 'born before time' and 'always born' are both true, but Gregory calls the latter 'truer' because it more clearly shows a generation without beginning or end and perfect, blocking heretical cavils. 'We cannot say always being born' means it is less fitting for expressing the truth, not that it is false. With Origen it can be said rightly: not that generation is repeated daily, but that the nativity is eternal.
claims: Both 'born before time' and 'always born' are true.
'Always born' expresses the truth more clearly against heretics.
'Always being born' is acceptable if understood as eternal, not repeated, nativity.

pll1d9c4-d1e3702.summary: Cites Hilary, De Trinitate VII, on John 6:58: the living God's eternal nature means that what is born of him can only be living, so the Son has life through the living Father. Here Hilary says the Son 'is born.'
claims: What is born of the living God is living.
The Son has life in himself through the living Father.
Hilary uses the present 'is born.'

pll1d9c4-d1e3730.summary: Cites Hilary on John 5:26: the living Son born of the living Father has a perfect nativity without novelty of nature, not from nothing, living in the living by unity of nature.
claims: The Son born of the living Father has a perfect birth without novelty.
The Son is not from nothing.

pll1d9c4-d1e3751.summary: Cites Hilary: in God all that is lives, since God is life; from life only the living can come, and birth is by power, not derivation. So the Son has nativity, not change.
claims: God is life, and what is born of life lives.
The Son's nativity involves no change.

pll1d9c4-d1e3763.summary: Cites Hilary, De Trinitate IX: the Father gives the Son to be as much as he is, and imparts to him the image of unbegottenness by the mystery of nativity, generating him from himself in his own form. Here Hilary uses the present 'generates.'
claims: The Father gives the Son to be as great as he is.
The Father begets the Son from himself in his own form.

pll1d9c4-d1e3781.summary: Concludes: the Son was born of the Father before time and is always being born, but more fittingly 'always born'; he is eternal and coeternal with the Father, his author. The Father is author of the Son by generation, to be shown later; both are eternal, but the Father without author, since unbegotten, and the Son not, since born.
claims: The Son is born before time and always born.
'Always born' is more fitting.
The Son is coeternal with the Father, his author.
The Father is eternal without author; the Son is eternal from an author.

pll1d9c4-d1e3785.summary: Cites Hilary, De Trinitate XII: being eternal without author differs from being coeternal with an author. Where the Father is author there is nativity, and from an eternal author an eternal nativity. Not every eternal thing is unborn. If anything of eternity were lacking to the Son, it would be lacking to the author, since begetting and being born are equally infinite. There is no interval between generation and nativity.
claims: Being eternal without an author differs from being coeternal with an author.
From an eternal author there is an eternal nativity.
Not everything eternal is unbegotten.
There is no interval between the Father's generating and the Son's nativity.

pl-l1d9c4.summary: Asks whether, since the generation is eternal, one should say the Son 'is always being born,' 'is always born,' or 'will always be born.' Gregory prefers 'always born' (semper natus), since 'always being born' suggests imperfection. Augustine reads 'today' in Ps 2:7 as the eternal present, and Chrysostom as birth from the Father's essence. But Origen says 'always being born,' like brightness from light, while Augustine in the 83 Questions says 'born' is better than 'always being born.' Lombard reconciles them: 'always born' is more fitting and clearer against heretics, but 'always being born' is true if understood as eternal nativity, not repetition. Hilary also speaks of the Son being born of the living Father. Conclusion: the Son was born before time and is always being born, but more fittingly 'always born'; he is coeternal with the Father, his author, the Father being without author and the Son not. With Hilary, being eternal without an author differs from being coeternal with an author, and generation and nativity have no interval between them.
claims: The Son's generation has neither beginning nor end.
'Always born' is the most fitting expression; 'always being born' is true when understood as eternal, non-repeated nativity.
'Today' in Ps 2:7 signifies the eternal present.
The Son is coeternal with the Father, who is his author.
The Father is eternal without an author; the Son is eternal from an author.
There is no interval between the Father's generating and the Son's being born.
